Executive Summary
China has made remarkable economic and social progress over the past 45 years, eliminating
absolute rural poverty in 2020 and registering substantial improvements in many social indicators,
including those for health and education.
1 China has entered a new era in its development, with
the Government now aiming to transition from 40 years of rapid economic expansion to a new
focus on “high-quality” development.
2
In this context, China is focused on ensuring its development is innovation-driven, coordinated,
green, open and shared by all. This vision is substantially aligned with the 2030 Agenda for
Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). China is currently
finalizing its 15th Five Year Plan (FYP) for Economic and Social Development (2026-2030). The
next five years align with the final five years of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
and China’s push towards high-quality development will likely remain the country’s top priority,
while China’s development success is essential for global achievement of the SDGs.
As per the Third Plenum,
3 China will focus on economic structural reform that leads to “greater
social fairness and justice and increased wellbeing”, as the stated ultimate goal, leveraging
innovation and new emerging sectors as new drivers of growth. This would include a focus on
expanding access to and the quality of social services and working to close development gaps. It
will also build on China’s progress in the green energy transition and combatting climate change
through increased investments in these sectors and accelerating the transition of its electricity grid.
China is both the world’s largest developing economy and the second biggest economy. As such,
China’s growth has the potential to benefit much of the world through trade, investments,
technological transfers and engagement in global sustainable development efforts. China has long
been a strong advocate of South-South cooperation and has put forward initiatives such as the Belt
and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Global Development Initiative (GDI), as its offer to contribute
to SDG progress in other developing countries.
In response to China’s new development trajectory and based on widespread consultations with
the Government of China, the 2026-2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation
Framework (Cooperation Framework) is structured around three interrelated and mutually
reinforcing Strategic Priorities. The Cooperation Framework is operationalised through four highlevel Outcomes towards which the UN system will concentrate its expertise and contributions.

The implementation of the Cooperation Framework will be coordinated through a Joint Steering
Committee (JSC), co-chaired by the vice minister of the Ministry of Commerce and the UN
Resident Coordinator, with membership from the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) in China
and relevant agencies within the Government. During implementation of the Cooperation
Framework, the JSC will meet annually to review progress towards the targeted results and
recommend strategic adjustments or new opportunities to accelerate action during the subsequent
period.
The UNCT will be configured in accordance with the principle of a “needs-based, tailored country
presence”, called for in the UN Development System repositioning resolution. The UNCT will
include both resident and non-resident entities who have committed through signature to
contributing towards at least one of the Cooperation Framework outcomes. The UNCT will also
draw on expertise from across the broader UN System, including its regional and global levels as
necessary to support successful implementation of the Cooperation Framework.4
Chapter 1: Country Progress Towards the 2030 Agenda
1.1 Country Context
Over the past four decades, China has experienced a rapid transformation, evolving from a
predominantly agrarian economy into the world’s second-largest economy. Since the launch of
reform and opening-up policies, China’s per capita GDP in real terms surged from USD 156 in
1978 to over USD 12,614 in 2023.
4 This economic growth has been accompanied by significant
improvements in life expectancy, education access, and living standards for its1.4 billion citizens.
China eliminated absolute rural poverty in 2020, with around 800 million people lifted out of
poverty5, almost half of whom were women.
6 China’s Human Development Index (HDI) reached
0.797 in 2023,
7 moving the country firmly into the high human development category.
China’s development model is transitioning from rapid economic expansion to high-quality
development, emphasizing sustainability, innovation, and inclusivity. As outlined in the 14th FiveYear Plan (FYP),
8 China aims to achieve a modern socialist economy by 2035 and develop into a
great modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced,
harmonious and beautiful by mid-21st century. This vision aligns with many parts of the 2030
Agenda for Sustainable Development, focusing on people-centred development, ecological
sustainability, and economic resilience.
Despite remarkable achievements, China faces complex challenges across the economic, social
and environmental dimensions of sustainable development. The benefits of China’s rapid
economic development have been unevenly distributed, with substantial interregional and ruralurban inequalities. China’s Gini coefficient of 0.467 (higher than the regional average) underlines
these challenges.
9
China’s population dynamics have shifted from incremental development to decremental
development, easing the pressure on resources and the environment. Population development
shows a trend characterized by low fertility rates, population ageing, and significant regional
differences in population growth and decline, which have brought new challenges. At the same
time, domestic and international migration has become an increasingly important factor for the
country’s development, bringing opportunities, but also challenges.
The country has made substantial progress with respect to gender equality and women’s
empowerment, including in the areas of improving access to education, healthcare, and
employment opportunities for women. China’s Gender Inequality Index was 0.186 in 2022,
ranking 47th out of 193 countries.

With regards to the environment, China has made significant progress in green energy, improving
air quality, reducing pollution and protecting biodiversity. Moreover, China continues to work to
fully integrate these new energy sources into the national electric grid, as well as raising energy
efficiency, which are needed to further reduce carbon emissions, achieve China’s dual carbon goals
of carbon peaking by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060, and keep the Paris Climate Agreement
alive.
China’s response to these challenges includes deepening economic reforms, fostering domestic
consumption, promoting technological self-reliance, and advancing green development. The focus
on innovation-driven growth, digital transformation, and rural revitalization aims to bridge
development gaps, reduce inequalities, and ensure sustainable prosperity. China has long been a
strong advocate and supporter of South-South Cooperation and has put forward initiatives like the
Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Global Development Initiative (GDI) as its offer to
contribute to global development and sustainability efforts. In particular, China has sought to align
GDI with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development to support global progress towards the
Sustainable Development Goals. China is willing to work with the international community to
steadily and orderly implement the Global Compact on Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, and
the Global Compact on Refugees.
1.2 China’s Vision for Sustainable Development
China’s development vision continues to evolve towards high-quality, people-centred, and
sustainable growth, aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The Government
has reaffirmed its commitment to transitioning from rapid economic expansion to sustainable,
innovation-driven development, underpinned by the Five New Development Concepts12:
• Innovation-Driven Growth: China has become a global leader in high-tech
manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital transformation, with research and
development expenditure reaching 2.65% of GDP in 2023.
13 Policies are focused on
building homegrown technological capabilities to drive long-term economic resilience,
with an increased emphasis placed on attracting more skilled migrants to accelerate this
innovation and growth.
• Coordinated Development: Addressing interregional disparities and rural-urban
inequalities remains a priority, with a strong focus on rural revitalization, urban-rural
integration, and reducing the income gap between rural and urban areas. The Government
has allocated 55% of rural revitalization funds to industrial development, supporting
infrastructure, education, and employment.
11 Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), Conclusions of the Ninth Periodic Review of China,
31 May 2023. 12 https://subsites.chinadaily.com.cn/npc/2021-12/24/c_693834.htm
13 Communique on National Expenditures on Science and Technology in 20236
• Green Development: China would strive to peak CO₂ emissions by 2030 and achieve
carbon neutrality by 2060. In 2023, renewable energy capacity additions accounted for 59%
of the world’s total, positioning China as the global leader in solar, wind, and hydroelectric
power.
• Open Development: Despite growing global trade tensions, China remains committed to
free trade agreements (FTAs) and regional economic integration, signing 23 FTAs with 30
countries and regions and has taken actions to support Open Development, for example by
implementing a zero-tariff policy on 100% of products originating from the LDCs with
which it has diplomatic ties from 1 December 2024.
• Shared Development: Poverty eradication efforts have shifted towards consolidating and
building upon the results of poverty elimination and promoting comprehensive rural
revitalization, with contributory and non-contributory pension schemes covering over 1.06
billion people by the end of 2023.
14 The Government plans to continue to expand access,
ensuring universal coverage of high-quality and sufficient social protection services for all
Chinese citizens that require it.
Looking ahead, China aims to achieve socialist modernization by 2035 and develop into a great
modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious
and beautiful by mid-21st century 15, reinforcing its commitment to inclusive, green, and
innovation-led development.
1.3 Progress Towards the SDGs
China has made significant strides in accelerating progress towards the Sustainable Development
Goals (SDGs). The country achieved a key objective of SDG 1 when it eradicated absolute rural
poverty in 2020, lifting over 770 million people out of poverty since the 1970s—a milestone that
accounts for 75% of global poverty reduction during this period. The rural revitalization strategy
continues to address the imbalance between urban and rural development and promote balanced
development across the country.
14 The contributory scheme refers to the employee scheme in which 521.22 million people are enrolled, while the non-contributory scheme refers
to the household scheme in which 545.22 million people are enrolled. 15 https://english.www.gov.cn/news/top_news/2017/10/18/content_281475912476280.htm7
Figure 1: UN DESA SDG Tracker
In the areas of food security and nutrition (SDG2), China has attained self-sufficiency in staple
foods, significantly reducing hunger and malnutrition. The prevalence of undernourishment has
declined to below 2.5% in recent years. Since 1990, China has recorded significant reductions in
stunting and wasting of children under 5 years of age. Meanwhile new challenges have emerged,
as childhood overweight and obesity rates have reached 10.4% of children under 6 years old in
2017.
16
In health (SDG 3), China has achieved near universal medical insurance coverage, with 94.6% of
the population ensured in 2023.
17 There has been a sustained increase in life expectancy at birth,
from 71.4 years in 2000 to 78.6 years in 2023. Maternal and child health indicators have improved
significantly, with maternal mortality dropping to 15.1 per 100,000, neonatal mortality (NMR),
infant mortality and under-five mortality (U5MR) rates reduced to, respectively 2.8, 4.5 and 6.2
per 1,000 live births in 2023, although disparities between rural and urban areas remain (with rural
NMR and U5MR being 1.9 and 1.8 times those or urban areas).
18 Targeted infectious diseases are
also under control. Yet major challenges remain, notably health inequalities between different
population groups and geographical locations, accelerated population ageing, increasing burden of
non-communicable diseases and their risk factors, existing communicable diseases, environmental
degradation, and a relatively weak primary healthcare system. The "Healthy China 2030" and the
“14th Five-Year National Health Plan”, among others, reaffirmed the Government’s commitment
to health as a public good and set the targets and road map for further improvements to health and
well-being in line with SDG 3.
In education (SDG 4), China has basically universalized preschool education, fully popularized
free, nine-year compulsory education, and significantly improved the enrolment rate in senior

rate of nine-year compulsory education, and the gross enrolment rate ofseniorsecondary education
reached 91.1%, 95.7%, and 91.8%, respectively. At the same time, approximately 3.16 million
upper secondary age (15 to 17 year-old) children were out of school, and only 58% of children in
rural areas complete upper secondary education, highlighting regional disparities. The government
is focusing its efforts on vocational training and digital literacy to prepare youth for the innovationdriven economy.
Gender equality (SDG 5) has advanced through legal reforms and targeted programmes, with
significant progress achieved. Targeted legal reforms and coordinated policy initiatives, including
the 2016 Anti-Domestic Violence Law, have contributed to a reduction in domestic violence in
China—with reported cases of physical and psychological violence against women falling to 8.6%
in 2020, a 5.2 percentage point decrease since 2010.
19 To further this progress, additional efforts
are needed in ensuring consistent enforcement, victim support, and addressing underlying social
norms. Women now constitute more than half of university students nationwide, reflecting their
expanding role in education and offering promising opportunities to further boost their
participation in frontier areas such as STEM and AI, and strengthen pathways into leadership roles
across academia, industry, and public service. Work remains in other areas, including reducing and
redistributing unpaid domestic care work, as women currently spend roughly 1.8 times the amount
of time as men on domestic chores.
20
China has been a global leader in integrating emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and
green technologies into its industrial sectors. This aligns with SDG 9’s focus on fostering
innovation. Despite progress, challenges remain in ensuring inclusivity and addressing disparities
in industrial development across regions.
Environmental sustainability (SDGs 6, 7, 13, 15) remains a priority. China leads globally in
renewable energy capacity, electric vehicle production, and afforestation efforts. Air quality has
improved, with PM2.5 levels declining by 34.8% since 2015. However, addressing coal
dependence, industrial pollution and biodiversity degradation and loss remain critical.
On SDG 16, China has made strides in promoting stability and reducing crime, with low violent
crime rates compared to global averages. The government has also invested in modernizing its
legal and judicial systems, enhancing the efficiency of dispute resolution and access to legal
services in urban and rural areas Meanwhile, China’s commitment to global peacekeeping,
demonstrated by its contributions to UN peacekeeping missions, highlights its international role in
promoting peace and security.
China’s contributions to SDG 17 include development cooperation, infrastructure investments
through the GDI, BRI, and South-South Cooperation, aimed at supporting stronger greener and
healthier sustainable global development.
21
While China continues to make progress across many areas of the SDGs, the ability to tell an
evidence-based story on its achievements is constrained due to persistent data gaps. In 2025,

1.4 Opportunities and Challenges
While China’s progress is commendable, several challenges persist. The urban-rural income ratio,
though improved, still reflects substantial inequality, with urban incomes averaging more than 2.34
times rural incomes in 2024.
The demographic shift towards an ageing population poses risks to economic productivity and
social services.
Environmental challenges include air and water pollution, biodiversity loss, and the need for a just
transition to a low-carbon economy. Climate change impacts, such as extreme weather events,
threaten food security and public health.
Addressing these issues requires comprehensive reforms, enhanced social protection, inclusive
economic policies, stronger environmental governance, and enhanced collection and analysis of
disaggregated data and statistics to inform evidence-based policy formulation.
While China’s development has been highly inclusive, challenges remain in “leaving no one
behind.” The UN analysis during the development of the Cooperation Framework identified a
number of groups who are more at risk of being left behind in China. These include, for example,
rural migrant workers in urban areas, people living in relatively remote regions with arduous
natural conditions, persons with disabilities, the growing elderly population, left-behind rural
children, children and women in difficulty, rural smallholder farmers, workers of new employment
forms, victims of human trafficking, and people living with HIV. These groups frequently overlap,
and the intersecting vulnerabilities leave some groups particularly marginalised. These groups
often also experience differentiated vulnerabilities to climate and disaster risks and impact from
disaster events (e.g. earthquakes, landslides, etc.).
Opportunitiesfor promoting ongoing progress toward SDG5 include improving women's and girls’
digital literacy and skills for innovation-driven development, as well as ensuring quality and
accessible social and legal services, including those addressing gender-based violence. More can
be done to promote women’s leadership in all sectors, to address the uneven distribution of unpaid
care work within families, and to promote women’s participation in green development and climate
change response. Importantly also, China is well positioned to enhance international cooperation
to address challenges affecting women globally.

Chapter 2: UN Development System Support to the 2030
Agenda in China
The Cooperation Framework is mutually owned and aligned with national development
priorities, the 2030 Agenda and the principles of the UN Charter. It is designed to embody the
spirit of partnerships to leverage strength and drive transformative change, making real the
collective promise to leave no one behind. It was developed through a consultative process, jointly
led by the Government through the Ministry of Commerce and the UN Resident Coordinator on
behalf of the UN Country Team (UNCT), involving a broad group of government entities. The
Cooperation Framework also builds upon the lessons learned and recommendations from the
external evaluation of the Cooperation Framework covering the period of 2021-2025 and tailors
its proposed interventions and activitiesto be in line with China’s changing development landscape.
The Cooperation Framework serves as the core accountability tool between the UNCT and the
Government, as well as between and among UNCT members for collectively owned development
results. It also shapes the configuration of UN assets required inside and outside the country.
United Nations entity-specific country programmes are derived from the Cooperation Framework.
Based on the UN system’s expertise and comparative advantages and its normative agenda, the
Cooperation Framework reflects: (a) the expectations national stakeholders have of the UN
development system’s contribution to national development; (b) a shared agreement of the
strategic priorities and contributions of the United Nations, derived from the theory of change; and
(c) the strategic partners with whom the UN system will work in pursuit of development progress.
2.1 Cooperation Framework Strategic Priorities
The 2026-2030 Cooperation Framework is designed to align with the national development agenda
of the Government of China, as outlined in the draft 15th Five-Year Plan, to support the
achievement of the 2030 Agenda.
The Cooperation Framework is structured around three Strategic Priorities, which are pillars
wherein the UN system will support China in its transformation and progress in the economic,
social and environmental dimensions of sustainable development, with a particular focus on equity
and leaving no one behind.
24
Strategic Priority 1: HIGH QUALITY PEOPLE-CENTRED DEVELOPMENT AND
SHARED PROSPERITY
Aiming to support China’s goal of achieving universal access to high quality social services
and social protection, including family and child friendly policies, to improve the quality
of life of all people in China, whilstsupporting China’s goal of achieving innovation-driven,
24 These will be reviewed carefully by the UN in China and the Government after the release of the 15th Five Year Plan to identify ways to further
enhance alignment.11
sustainable and shared economic development and transformation, leading to increased
quality employment and livelihood opportunities.
Strategic Priority 2: CLIMATE ACTION AND ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY.
Aiming to support China’s goals and contribution to addressing the three major risks of
climate change, biodiversity loss, and environmental pollution.
Strategic Priority 3: PARTNERSHIPS TO ACCELERATE SUSTAINABLE
DEVELOPMENT.
Aiming to leverage China’s commitment to international development cooperation and
financing, including through the Global Development Initiative, to advance global progress
on the SDGs and multilateral environmental agreements.
2.2 Cooperation Framework Outcomes
The Cooperation Framework is operationalised by high-level Outcomes, which are underpinned
by a specific theory of change that articulates the pathway to achieve the desired result through
overcoming the key challenges and grasping development opportunities.
The United Nations system will support China towards achieving the Outcomes of the Cooperation
Framework, responding to emerging challenges, and accelerating the implementation of the SDGs
through its extensive system of organizations, global knowledge community, normative
frameworks and mechanisms reflected in multilateral conventions and treaties, and capacity to
identify and transfer international best practices and catalytic solutions for development.
In recognition of the evolving development landscape in China and the country’s depth of
capacities and resources, the United Nations system will accelerate its shift to a much greater
intensity of strategic, high reach and high impact policy advice, evidence-based analysis, research,
and cutting-edge technical inputs based on scientific evidence-based approaches.
In doing so, in mutual agreement with the Government, the United Nations system will support
the modelling and the showcasing of innovative solutions to development opportunities with
government agencies, local governments and the private sector.
Leveraging its global, regional and national networks, platforms and expertise, the United Nations
system in China will serve to strengthen development and humanitarian cooperation and
knowledge and experience sharing between China and other countries
The four Cooperation Framework Outcomes are interrelated, mutually reinforcing and
multisectoral. Together, they offer the opportunity to support China to accelerate progress towards
the achievement of the (draft) 15th Five-Year Plan goals and, ultimately, Agenda 2030 and the
SDGs. The UN contribution to the achievement of the Outcomes will be operationalised through
Outputs.12
The Outcomes and the major areas of the United Nations system’s contributions to them are guided
by the following principles:
i. Leaving no one behind: To identify and reach those who may not have benefited
from the sustained inclusive and sustainable economic growth and social and
progress. This could include countries that have been left out from overall
sustainable development progress.
ii. Right to development and dignity as a normative foundation of the United Nations.
iii. Gender equality and women’s empowerment: To put gender equality at the heart
of cooperation and sustainable development, driving the equal, active and
meaningful participation of both women and men.
iv. Sustainability: Ensuring the interconnections among the social, economic and
environmental dimensions of sustainable development and applying social and
environmental standards across all programming cooperation.
v. Resilience: Of systems, programmes, communities, individuals and the
environment.
vi. Accountability: To support national development priorities and improving the lives
of people in China, particularly those most vulnerable and at risk of being left
further behind.13
UN Contribution to Outcome 1
The UN Offer: Build capacity of the Government and other stakeholders with the objective of
increasing the proportion of people that benefit from high quality service. Technical assistance
will be provided to strengthen the implementation of harmonized laws, policies, frameworks and
regulations in support of universal and high-quality social services.
The United Nations will support the Government of China to develop policies, programmes and
mechanisms to ensure access to high-quality, affordable, inclusive, and climate-resilient social
services and social protection, improving well-being for all and leaving no one behind. Working
in close collaboration with the Government of China and key stakeholders, the UN will support
strengthening health and nutrition systems, enhancing education and learning opportunities,
reinforcing social protection mechanisms, addressing demographic shifts, improving skilled
labour mobility management and fostering social inclusion. These interventions align with the
preliminary priorities of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030 25 ) and contribute to the
achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
The UN will continue to work with national partners to strengthen the resilience and inclusivity of
China’s health system. Technical support and policy dialogues will help ensure primary healthcare
is the foundation of an integrated service delivery system that provides gender-responsive and
quality services across the life course and is able to manage the demographic transition and
changing disease burdens. This includes strengthening the safe and nutritious food supply for
maternal, child, and adolescent health, strengthening disease control, as well as services for older
persons and individuals affected by non-communicable and communicable diseases. Attention will
be given to sexual and reproductive health, including family planning and fertility care. Through
technical cooperation and policy reform, the UN will assist in improving equitable health financing
strategies to reduce financial barriers and expand universal health coverage, particularly for
vulnerable populations. Public health security will be reinforced through improved monitoring,
early warning systems, and enhanced collaboration on health threats, ensuring timely responses to
potential outbreaks and the long-term sustainability of disease prevention and control measures.
25 The 15th FYP will not be adopted until March 2026.14
In addition to coping with major communicable diseases such as HIV, tuberculosis and viral
hepatitis, the UN will also work to address the rise of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), which
contribute to 89.3% of all deaths in China. The growing prevalence of NCDs, including
hypertension, diabetes, and obesity, among others, as well as their risk factors, reduce health and
the ability of people to live healthy lives, particularly as they age, along with a loss in productive
labour and a significant burden on the health care system. NCDs are not just a health issue, but
also a development issue.
Education remains a cornerstone of equitable development, and the UN will collaborate with
government partners to enhance the inclusivity, resilience, and quality of the education system.
This includes technical and financial support to improve education policies, modernise curricula,
and develop teacher training programmes. Efforts will be made to improve access to quality
learning, particularly for children with disabilities, children from economically disadvantaged
families, children affected by migration, and other special groups, ensuring that all students benefit
from an inclusive education framework. The UN will also support the digital transformation of
education systems, integrating innovative education technologies to expand access to learning
opportunities, while ensuring parameters and protections are in place to guarantee children’s safety
online. Vocational education and skills development will be strengthened to prepare young people
for emerging labour markets, with particular attention to ensuring women’s participation in
Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics fields and emerging and digital technologies,
including green technologies. Additionally, advocacy for life skills, including emergency response
skills, and improvement of lifelong learning for young people, adolescents and adults will be
prioritized for continuing skills acquisition, upskilling and reskilling, particularly in remote areas,
to equip all women and men with essential knowledge and competencies to engage in quality
socio-economic development.
As part of its commitment to social protection, the UN will work with Government counterparts
to expand universal social protection coverage throughout the life course. Technical assistance will
be provided to strengthen legal frameworks and financial management, improve programme
design and implementation of social assistance programmes and social insurance schemes, and
ensure that pension systems, social assistance, medical insurance, maternity insurance and
unemployment benefits are inclusive of rural migrant workers, workers of new employment forms,
women, children, persons with disabilities, people living with HIV and other vulnerable
populations. The UN will also work with the Government of China to integrate the social
protection system with climate adaptation and mitigation strategies, ensuring that policies are
adaptive to climate induced economic and other shocks. By supporting the development of
evidence-based vulnerability monitoring systems, the UN will contribute to informed policy
decision-making, ensuring that everyone in need in China is able to access and benefit from
targeted social protection schemes.
With China experiencing significant demographic transitions, the UN will work with partners to
develop evidence-based policies to address population ageing and low fertility and reap the
potential of human development. This includes supporting the expansion of early childhood

2.3 Synergies and Sustainability between Cooperation Framework

The three Strategic Priorities and four Outcomes are interdependent and integrated for sustainable
development. Progress towards the achievement of one Outcome will both contribute to and
require progress in other Outcomes. The synergies between the four Outcomes are clearly aligned
with the five interrelated dimensions of the 2030 Agenda – People, Prosperity, Planet, Peace and
Partnerships – and the goals of the draft 15th Five-Year Plan.
The synergies between the four Cooperation Framework Outcomes are reflective of the mutually
reinforcing nature of the SDGs and are highlighted across the planned UN contributions to the
outcomes detailed in section 2.2. Investing in improving education, lifelong learning, health and
nutrition in Outcome 1 will contribute to the economic growth aims of Outcome 2 through
enhanced productivity and skills. Strengthening social protection mechanisms - particularly for the
most vulnerable - will not only contribute to the objectives of Outcome 1 but will also help to
strengthen people’s potential to contribute to and benefit from economic diversification and growth
under Outcome 2 and to live more environmentally sustainable practices in Outcome 3.
Supporting strengthened environmental and natural resource management including an expanded
circular economy under Outcome 3, will contribute to the objectives of Outcome 2 regarding
sustainable and green-led economic development and improved livelihoods, and vice versa.
The aims of Outcome 4 on strengthening partnerships and commitment to drive sustainable
development are foundations for the other three Outcomes.
Sustainability of the results and impact of all Outcomes beyond 2030 will be ensured through close
alignment between the Cooperation Framework and national development priorities and plans.
The UN will leverage its well-established partnerships at the country level to ensure full coownership of national partners for the implementation of the Cooperation Framework.24
At the programme level, sustainability will be ensured by clearly articulated, and regularly
revisited, exit strategies and risk mitigation plans that are embedded in programme design.

develop innovative pilot/demonstration projects, which aim to test and promote innovative

where UN entities collaborate with each other to leverage on their complementarities regarding a
particular intervention. Building on this finding, the UN will strengthen integration of UN entities’
normative and programmatic work through enhanced collaboration.
2.4 UN Comparative Advantages and UNCT Configuration
Over the past 45 years, the UN System has become a longstanding trusted partner of the
Government of China. According to the External Evaluation of the UN Cooperation Framework
2021-2025, the UN continues to be a valuable partner in China and there continues to be a demand
for engagement around a number of development areas focused on SDG progress using a range of
modalities, including pilot project implementation, technical assistance, and policy support, among
others. The UN also continuesto be recognized by Chinese partnersfor its high-quality programme
implementation, including its strong emphasis on monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL)
The UN takes a people-centred approach that places a particular emphasis on vulnerable groups,
and emphasizes gender equality and women’s empowerment, as well as relevant, effective and
sustainable development cooperation, which is aligned with many parts of the Government’s
national development agenda, in particular its emphasis on “high-quality” and “people-centred”

Chapter 3: Cooperation Framework Implementation Plan
3.1Cooperation Framework Governance
The implementation of the Cooperation Framework will be coordinated through a National/UN
Joint Steering Committee. The Joint Steering Committee (JSC) will be co-chaired by the leader of
the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China and the United Nations Resident
Coordinator. Its membership will include the Resident Coordinator’s Office (RCO), UNCT

results and recommend strategic adjustments or new opportunities to accelerate action during the
subsequent period.
3.2 Risk Management and Assumptions
There are three main overall risks to the successful implementation of the Cooperation Framework,
which cut across all the Outcome areas.
The first risk relates to the UN System being unable to ensure and continue to maintain its own
added value and effectively use its own strategic and technical policy support to help China achieve
“high-quality development”, as a result of the UN’s resource constraints. The Cooperation
Framework aims to position the UN as a strategic and technical policy advisor to the Government
on the complex development challenges it is facing as it moves from a “high-speed” to a “highquality” development model. To mitigate the risk, the UN in China will focus on China’s actual
development stage, provide strategic and technical policy support to China, and effectively
introduce high-quality development experience through field projects where funds are sufficient,
to further help the Government meet the Chinese people’s desire for a better life. Additionally, the
UN will undertake actions to better mobilize and strategically use the expertise and resources that
exist across the system at regional and global levels.
The second risk relates to the UN being unable to mobilize the funding needed to implement the
Cooperation Framework. To manage the risk, the UN and the Government will collaborate to
mobilize the needed resources, commensurate with China’sstatus asthe largest developing country
and an upper-middle income country (see section 3.3 ‘Resourcing the Cooperation Framework’).
The third risk relates to the potential occurrence of external events, including pandemics and
natural disasters, which would have a negative impact on the UN and the Government’s possibility
to continue implementation of ongoing activities, as well as on development gains already made.
The activities related to the strengthening of social protection systems outlined in this Cooperation
Framework will further contribute to decreasing the vulnerability of people when faced with
shocks caused by epidemics, natural disasters or other emergencies.27
3.3 Resourcing the Cooperation Framework
In line with national legal frameworks and policies and to the extent possible under the law, the
Government will support the UN system’s agencies in efforts to raise funds requirements to meet
some of the needs of the Cooperation Framework.
Based on initial estimates, full implementation of this Cooperation Framework, for the entire 5-
year period, is estimated to be US$744 million, with the following estimated breakdown between
the three Strategic Priority Areas:
• Strategic Priority 1: $421 million
• Strategic Priority 2: $249 million
• Strategic Priority 3: $74 million
Achievement of the Cooperation Framework results will require a concerted resource mobilization
strategy driven jointly by the Joint Steering Committee and the UNCT.
Sources of funding include UN entities’ regular/core resources and other/non-core resources that
UN entities are able to mobilize on the strength of the strategies and expected results. Othersources
of funding to support Cooperation Framework implementation include from the Government of
China, vertical and thematic funds (including the Global Environment Facility), Joint SDG Funds,
the corporate sector and other bilateral contributions, among others.
The UN in China will continue to leverage a wide range of diverse partners to ensure that the
Cooperation Framework is adequately funded, and these strategies will be described in more detail
in the resource mobilization strategy document.
3.4 Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) is a key priority for the UNCT entities,
with a special focus on prioritizing victims' rights and creating an environment in which sexual
exploitation and abuse (SEA) do not occur. SEA is unacceptable behaviour and is prohibited for
UN personnel and UN implementing partners. The UN system entities will therefore pursue all
appropriate means to protect against, prevent and respond to SEA, and will require a similar
commitment from its partners.
In delivering on the obligations articulated in the present Cooperation Framework, the UNCT and
the Government of China affirm their commitment to preventing and responding to reports of SEA
in connection with their personnel involved in common/joint projects. It is understood that this
would entail the need to: (i) adhere to common values on PSEA, (ii) take preventative measures
against SEA, (iii) investigate allegations, and (iv) take appropriate corrective action when incidents
occur, including providing support to victims in accordance with a victim centred approach28

The Cooperation Framework Outcomes and outputs are ambitious and span a broad range of
development issues that are cross-cutting in nature. To deliver on these, the UNCT will need to
draw upon the capacities across the UN System. Specifically, the UNCT will be configured in
accordance with the principle of a “needs-based, tailored country presence”, called for in the UN
development system repositioning resolution. Based on an assessment of the capacities and
expertise needed to deliver on the Cooperation Framework, the UNCT will include UN entities
identified through the assessment and which have committed through signature to contributing
towards at least one of the Cooperation Framework Outcomes. While the main responsibility for
the implementation of the Cooperation Framework will rest with the UNCT members, additional
assets and expertise from across the broader UN system, including its regional and global levels
will be mobilised to support as necessary. This additional expertise will be essential for the UN to
fulfil its role as a provider of cutting-edge advice. Resources from the broader UN system will be
utilised on a needs basis, with the UN Resident Coordinator playing a key role in mobilising
expertise. The table below illustrates the collaborative capacity of all members of the UNCT and

ANNEX 3 LEGAL ANNEX
Whereas the Government of China (hereinafter referred to as “the Government”) has entered into
the agreements listed below with the United Nations, including its Funds, Programmes and other
subsidiary organs, and other organizations of the United Nations system (“UN System
Organizations”), which are applicable to their programme activities in China (the “UN
Agreements”) under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (the
“Cooperation Framework”);
2. Whereas the UN Agreements, together with the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities
of the United Nations of 13 February 1946 (the “General Convention”) and/or the Convention on
the Privileges and Immunities of the Specialized Agencies of 21 November 1947 (the “Specialized
Agencies Convention”) as applicable, form the primary existing legal basis for the relationship
between the Government and each UN System Organization for supporting the country to deliver
on the Cooperation Framework, and are non-exhaustive and without prejudice to any other legal
instruments the Government may enter into, including additional agreements with UN System
Organizations for the purpose of their activities in the country:
a. With United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have entered into Standard Basic
Assistance Agreement (SBAA), which was signed by both parties on 29 June 1979.
b. With the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) a Basic Cooperation Agreement (BCA)
concluded between the Government and UNICEF on 22 June 1981.
c. With the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) a
Framework Agreement concluded between the Government and UNHCR on 1 December 1995.
d. With the World Food Programme (WFP) a Basic Agreement concerning assistance from the
World Food Programme, which Agreement was signed by the Government and WFP on 4 October
1980.
e. With the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the Programme Agreement between
UNFPA and the Government of China, signed on 9 September 1980.
f. With the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the Standard
Basic Assistance Agreement between the United Nations Development Programme and the
Government, signed on 29 June 1979 and entered into force on 24 June 1985, applies mutatis
mutandis to UNIDO projects and programmes in China.
g. With the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) the Host Country
Agreement for the opening of the FAO Representation in China was signed by the Government
and FAO on 25 May 1982.
h. With the International Organization for Migration (IOM) the Agreement between the
International Organization for Migration and the Government of the People’s Republic of China
on the establishment of an office of the International Organization for Migration in China, signed
by the Government and IOM on 22 August 2017.39
i. With the World Health Organization (WHO) the Basic Agreement concluded between the
Government and WHO on 4 October 1982.
j. With the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific
(ESCAP), the Agreement Regarding the Headquarters of the Asian and Pacific Centre for
Agricultural Engineering and Machinery (later renamed Centre for Sustainable Agricultural
Mechanization – CSAM) signed on 19 November 2003.
k. With the International Fund for Agricultural Development of the United Nations (IFAD),
the Agreement Between the Government of the People’s Republic of China and IFAD on the
Establishment of the IFAD’s Country Office signed on 28 August 2017 and the Agreement
Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development that the Government signed and
acceded on 15 January 1980.
l. With the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the agreement between the
Government and the UNEP on the establishment of the UNEP Office in the People’s Republic of
China, signed on 29 May 2003 in Nairobi.
m. With the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO),
the Memorandum of Understanding on Cooperation Between the Government of the People’s
Republic of China and UNESCO (2017-2020) signed on 13 May 2017.
n. With the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN Habitat), the 2017-2021
Framework of Cooperation between UN Habitat and the Ministry of Housing and Urban
Development of the People’s Republic of China, signed on 15 May 2017.
o. With the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), the Strategic
Partnership with the National Health and Family Planning Commission of the People’s Republic
of China (2013- 2014) came into effect in September 2013, underpinned by UNAIDS’
establishment by ECOSOC resolutions 1994/24 and 1995/2 and governed by the Convention on
the Privileges and Immunities of the Specialized Agencies of 21st November 1947 (the
“Specialized Agencies Convention”).
p. With the International Labour Organization (ILO), the “Agreement Concerning the
Establishment of an Area Office of the International Labour Organization at Beijing”, signed on
27 November 1984.

Resource mobilisation
In full consultation with the government, the UN System agencies will provide support to the
development and implementation of activities within the Cooperation Framework, which may
include technical support, cash assistance, supplies, commodities and equipment, procurement
services, transport, funds for advocacy, research and studies, consultancies, programme
development, monitoring and evaluation, training activities and staff support. In mutual agreement
with the Government, Part of the UN System entities’ support may be provided to nongovernmental organisations as agreed within the framework of the individual workplans and
project documents.
Additional support may include access to UN organisation-managed global information systems,
the network of the UN System agencies’ country offices and specialised information systems,
including rosters of consultants and providers of development services, and access to the support
provided by the network of UN specialised agencies, funds and programmes. The UN System
agencies shall appoint staff and consultant for programme development, programme support,
technical assistance, as well as monitoring and evaluation activities.
Subject to annual reviews and progress in the implementation of the programme, the UN System
agencies’ funds are distributed by calendar year and in accordance with the Cooperation
Framework. These budgets will be reviewed and further detailed in the workplans and project
documents. By mutual consent between the Government and the UN development system entities,
funds not earmarked by donors to UN development system agencies for specific activities may be
re-allocated to other programmatically equally worthwhile activities.
The Government is willing to provide necessary support for mobilisation of the resources for the
implementation of the UNSDCF programmes in China, while ensuring alignment with Chinese
laws and regulations.
Monitoring and evaluation
Implementing Partners agree to cooperate with the UN system agencies for monitoring all
activities supported by cash transfers and will facilitate access to relevant financial records and
personnel responsible for the administration of cash provided by the UN system agencies. To that
effect, Implementing Partners agree to the following:
1. Periodic on-site reviews and spot checks of their financial records by the UN system agencies
or their representatives, as appropriate, and as described in specific clauses of their engagement
documents/ contracts with the UN system agencies,

guidance for site visits and field monitoring,
3. Special or scheduled audits. Each UN organization, in collaboration with other UN system
agencies (where so desired and in consultation with the respective coordinating Ministry) will
establish an annual audit plan, giving priority to audits of Implementing Partners with large
amounts of cash assistance provided by the UN system agencies, and those whose financial
management capacity needs strengthening.

All cash transfers to an Implementing Partner are based on the Work Plans (WPs11) agreed
between the Implementing Partner and the UN System agencies.
Cash transfers for activities detailed in work plans (WPs) can be made by the UN System agencies
using the following modalities:
1. Cash transferred directly to the Implementing
Partner:
a. Prior to the start of activities (direct cash transfer), or
b. After activities have been completed (reimbursement);
2. Direct payment to vendors or third parties for obligations incurred by the Implementing
Partners on the basis of requests signed by the designated official of the Implementing Partner;
3. Direct payments to vendors or third parties for obligations incurred by UN System agencies in
support of activities agreed with Implementing Partners.
Where cash transfers are made to the [national institution], the [national institution] shall transfer
such cash promptly to the Implementing Partner.
Direct cash transfers shall be requested and released for programme implementation periods not
exceeding three months. Reimbursements of previously authorised expenditures shall be requested
and released quarterly or after the completion of activities. The UN System agencies shall not be
obligated to reimburse expenditure made by the Implementing Partner over and above the
authorised amounts. Following the completion of any activity, any balance of funds shall be
refunded or programmed by mutual agreement between the Implementing Partner and the UN
System agencies.
Cash transfer modalities, the size of disbursements, and the scope and frequency of assurance
activities may depend on the findings of a review of the public financial management capacity in
the case of a Government Implementing Partner, and of an assessment of the financial management
capacity of the non-UN Implementing Partner. A qualified consultant, such as a public accounting
firm, selected by the UN System agencies may conduct such an assessment, in which the43
Implementing Partner shall participate. The Implementing Partner may participate in the selection
of the consultant.
Cash transfer modalities, the size of disbursements, and the scope and frequency of assurance
activities may be revised in the course of programme implementation based on the findings of
programme monitoring, expenditure monitoring and reporting, and audits.
A standard Fund Authorisation and Certificate of Expenditures (FACE) report, reflecting the
activity lines of the work plan (WP), will be used by Implementing Partners to request the release
of funds, or to secure the agreement that [UN organisation] will reimburse or directly pay for
planned expenditure. The Implementing Partners will use the FACE to report on the utilisation of
cash received. The Implementing Partner shall identify the designated official(s) authorised to
provide the account details, request and certify the use of cash. The FACE will be certified by the
designated official(s) of the Implementing Partner. Cash transferred to Implementing Partners
should be spent for the purpose of activities and within the timeframe as agreed in the work plans
(WPs) only.
Cash received by the Government and national NGO Implementing Partners shall be used in
accordance with established national regulations, policies and procedures consistent with
international standards, in particular ensuring that cash is expended for activities as agreed in the
work plans (WPs), and ensuring that reports on the utilisation of all received cash are submitted to
[UN organisation] within six months after receipt of the funds. Where any of the national
regulations, policies and procedures are not consistent with international standards, the UN System
agency financial and other related rules and system agency regulations, policies and procedures
will apply.
In the case of international NGO/CSO and IGO Implementing Partners cash received shall be used
in accordance with internationalstandards in particular ensuring that cash is expended for activities
as agreed in the work plans (WPs), and ensuring that reports on the full utilisation of all received
cash are submitted to [UN organisation] within six months after receipt of the funds.
To facilitate scheduled and special audits, each Implementing Partner receiving cash from [UN
organisation] will provide UN System agency or its representative with timely access to:
• all financial records which establish the transactional record of the cash transfers provided
by [UN System agency], together with relevant documentation;
• all relevant documentation and personnel associated with the functioning of the
Implementing Partner’s internal control structure through which the cash transfers have
passed. The findings of each audit will be reported to the Implementing Partner and [UN
organisation]. Each Implementing Partner will furthermore:
• Receive and review the audit report issued by the auditors.
• Provide a timely statement of the acceptance or rejection of any audit recommendation to
the [UN organisation] that provided cash (and where the SAI has been identified to conduct
the audits,
• add: and to the SAI) so that the auditors include these statements in their final audit report
before submitting it to [UN organisation].44
• Undertake timely actions to address the accepted audit recommendations. Report on the
actions taken to implement accepted recommendations to the UN System agencies (and
where the SAI
• has been identified to conduct the audits, add: and to the SAI), on a quarterly basis (or as
locally agreed).
In case of direct cash transfer or reimbursement, the UN System agencies shall notify the
Implementing Partner of the amount approved by the UN System agencies and shall disburse funds
to the Implementing Partner in [here insert the number of days as per UN System agency schedule].
In case of direct payment to vendors or third parties for obligations incurred by the Implementing
Partners on the basis of requests signed by the designated official of the Implementing Partner; or
to vendors or third parties for obligations incurred by the UN System agencies in support of
activities agreed with Implementing Partners, the UN System agencies shall proceed with the
payment within [here insert the number of days as agreed by the UN System agencies].
The UN System agencies shall not have any direct liability under the contractual arrangements
concluded between the Implementing Partner and a third party vendor.
Where the UN System agencies and other UN System agency provide cash to the same
Implementing Partner, programme monitoring, financial monitoring and auditing will be
undertaken jointly or coordinated with those UN System agencies.
Audits, if any, will be commissioned by the UN System agencies and undertaken by private audit
services.
